# 12-Week Couch-to-5K Programme
### Client Profile & Key Considerations

**Client:** 24-year-old male | **Condition:** Exercise-induced asthma (EIA), controlled with a SABA (short-acting beta-agonist) inhaler | **Goal:** Complete a continuous 5K run | **GP Clearance:** Granted with specific guidance around warm-up quality and cold-air precautions.

---

## Standing Safety Protocols (Apply Every Session, Every Week)

Before diving into the programme itself, these non-negotiables must be embedded into every single session and reviewed with your client at the outset.

**Inhaler Protocol:** Your client should take 2 puffs of his SABA inhaler **15–20 minutes before every session** begins, as per standard EIA management guidance. He should carry the inhaler on his person at all times during training — not left in a bag, not in the car. Confirm this habit is established in week one and check in on it regularly.

**Cold Air Management:** Below approximately 10°C, your client should wear a lightweight buff or cold-air face mask over his nose and mouth during outdoor running. This warms and humidifies inhaled air before it reaches the airways, significantly reducing bronchospasm risk. On very cold or windy days (below 5°C), consider moving the session to a treadmill indoors. Always check the weather the day before and have an indoor contingency plan ready.

**Symptom Red Flags — Stop Immediately If:** chest tightness develops and does not ease within 60–90 seconds of slowing to a walk; two puffs of the SABA inhaler do not relieve symptoms within 10 minutes; the client experiences wheezing at rest, severe breathlessness disproportionate to effort, or any dizziness. In these situations, stop the session, sit the client upright, administer the inhaler, and call emergency services if there is no improvement. Document every episode and report to the GP.

**Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE):** Use the Borg 6–20 scale throughout. Running efforts should stay between RPE 11–14 (fairly light to somewhat hard) in the early phases, rising to RPE 14–16 in the final phase. If the client cannot speak in short sentences while running, he is working too hard and must slow down.

**Breathing Technique:** Coach nasal breathing during warm-ups and easy efforts wherever possible. Nasal breathing warms and filters air more effectively than mouth breathing. During harder running efforts, a relaxed mouth-breathing pattern is fine, but encourage rhythmic breathing (e.g., inhale for 3 steps, exhale for 2) to prevent shallow, panicked breathing patterns that can trigger or worsen bronchospasm.

## Programme Structure Overview

The 12 weeks are divided into three distinct phases, each building on the last.

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1: Foundation | 1–4 | Walk/run intervals, aerobic base, breathing habits |
| Phase 2: Development | 5–8 | Extended run intervals, reduced walk recovery |
| Phase 3: Consolidation | 9–12 | Continuous running, 5K target |

**Session Frequency:** 3 sessions per week with at least one full rest day between each running session. A suggested layout is Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday, giving adequate recovery while maintaining consistency.

**Warm-Up Protocol (Mandatory — Minimum 10 Minutes Every Session):** This is not optional for this client. A thorough warm-up is one of the most effective non-pharmacological strategies for reducing EIA severity. The warm-up should be structured as follows:

- *Minutes 1–3:* Brisk walking at a comfortable pace, focusing on relaxed nasal breathing and settling into a rhythm.
- *Minutes 3–6:* Dynamic mobility — leg swings (forward/back and lateral, 10 reps each leg), hip circles, arm circles, walking lunges with a torso twist (8 each side), and ankle rolls. Keep movement continuous and gentle.
- *Minutes 6–10:* Graduated intensity walking, building pace progressively so the heart rate rises gently. In weeks 5 onwards, the final 2 minutes of warm-up can include very light jogging at an easy conversational pace. The goal is to arrive at the first running interval with airways already open and the body warm.

**Cool-Down Protocol (Minimum 8 Minutes Every Session):** Abrupt cessation of exercise can also trigger late-phase bronchospasm. Always finish with 3–4 minutes of easy walking, then 4–5 minutes of static stretching targeting the calves, hip flexors, hamstrings, and chest/shoulders. Encourage slow, controlled breathing throughout the cool-down.

---

## Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)
### Goal: Establish the run/walk habit, build aerobic base, embed asthma management routines

The priority in this phase is not fitness — it is habit and safety. Your client needs to learn how his airways respond to exercise, build confidence, and develop the warm-up and breathing disciplines that will protect him throughout the programme. Running intervals are short and the walk recoveries are generous. Resist any temptation to progress faster than the plan dictates, even if your client feels good.

---

### Week 1

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session (excluding warm-up/cool-down):** 20 minutes

Each of the three sessions this week follows the same structure. After the full 10-minute warm-up protocol described above, your client will alternate between 1 minute of easy jogging and 2 minutes of brisk walking. Repeat this cycle 6–7 times to fill approximately 20 minutes of work. Finish with the full cool-down.

The jogging pace should feel almost embarrassingly easy — slower than he thinks he needs to go. If he can't hold a conversation, he's going too fast. The walk intervals are active recovery, not a stroll; maintain a purposeful pace to keep the heart rate from dropping too sharply.

**Coaching focus this week:** Spend time at the start of session one establishing the inhaler pre-treatment habit, checking he has it on his person, and walking through the red-flag symptoms together. Introduce the RPE scale and get him rating himself at the end of each run interval. Aim for RPE 11–12.

---

### Week 2

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 20–22 minutes

Increase the run interval to **90 seconds** of jogging followed by **2 minutes** of brisk walking. Repeat 6 times. The total running volume increases modestly but the walk recovery remains generous. The pace stays the same — easy and conversational.

**Coaching focus:** Begin introducing rhythmic breathing during the run intervals. Suggest a 3:2 pattern (3 steps inhale, 2 steps exhale) and let him experiment with it. Some clients find this natural; others need a few sessions. Don't force it, but plant the seed. Check in on cold-air management if temperatures have dropped since week one.

---

### Week 3

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 22–25 minutes

This week introduces a small variation across the three sessions to begin building adaptability.

**Session 1 and Session 2:** 90 seconds jogging / 90 seconds walking, repeated 8 times. The walk recovery shortens slightly for the first time, which is a meaningful step. Monitor his response carefully.

**Session 3:** 3 minutes jogging / 2 minutes walking, repeated 4 times. This is the first time he will sustain a 3-minute run. Pace must remain easy. If he struggles, it is almost certainly a pacing issue rather than a fitness ceiling — slow him down rather than shortening the interval.

**Coaching focus:** After session 3, have a brief debrief conversation. How did the 3-minute run feel? Were there any airway symptoms? This feedback loop is valuable for adjusting the programme if needed and for building his self-awareness as an asthmatic exerciser.

---

### Week 4

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 25 minutes

**Session 1:** 3 minutes jogging / 90 seconds walking, repeated 5 times.

**Session 2:** 5 minutes jogging / 2.5 minutes walking, repeated 3 times. This is a significant jump in continuous running duration. Pace accordingly — this should feel like RPE 12 at most.

**Session 3:** This is a consolidation session. Return to the week 3 session 3 format (3 minutes jogging / 2 minutes walking × 4) but aim for a slightly more confident, settled pace. The purpose is to reinforce what has been built before moving into Phase 2.

**End-of-Phase 1 Check-In:** Before moving to Phase 2, review the following with your client. Has he been consistent with pre-exercise inhaler use? Has he experienced any EIA episodes, and if so, what triggered them? Is he comfortable with the warm-up routine and can he execute it independently? Is his resting breathing comfortable and his recovery between sessions adequate? If there are any concerns, repeat week 4 before progressing.

---

## Phase 2: Development (Weeks 5–8)
### Goal: Extend continuous running intervals, reduce walk recovery, build aerobic confidence

Phase 2 is where the real aerobic development happens. Run intervals grow substantially and walk recoveries shrink. The client should now have a reliable warm-up habit and a good sense of his own pacing. Your role shifts slightly from safety educator to performance coach, though the asthma protocols remain fully in place.

---

### Week 5

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 25–28 minutes

**Session 1:** 5 minutes jogging / 3 minutes walking, repeated 3 times.

**Session 2:** 8 minutes jogging / 5 minutes walking, repeated 2 times. The 8-minute run is a landmark moment. Encourage him beforehand and remind him that pace is everything — slow and steady wins here.

**Session 3:** 5 minutes jogging / 3 minutes walking, repeated 3 times (same as session 1, consolidating the week's work).

**Coaching focus:** Introduce the concept of a "conversational pace test." During the 8-minute run in session 2, ask him a simple question mid-run. If he can answer in a short sentence without gasping, the pace is right. If he can't, slow down. This is a practical, real-time tool he can use independently.

---

### Week 6

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 28–30 minutes

**Session 1:** 5 minutes jogging / 3 minutes walking / 8 minutes jogging / 3 minutes walking / 5 minutes jogging. This is a pyramid-style session that totals 18 minutes of running with two walk breaks.

**Session 2:** 10 minutes jogging / 3 minutes walking / 10 minutes jogging. The first double-digit run interval. This is a significant milestone. Pace must be conservative — RPE 12–13.

**Session 3:** 20–22 minutes of easy continuous jogging if session 2 went well, or repeat session 1 if there were any airway concerns. Use your clinical judgement here based on his feedback.

**Coaching focus:** If he attempts the 22-minute continuous run in session 3, this is a good moment to discuss pacing strategy for longer efforts — starting slightly slower than feels necessary and finishing feeling like he had a little more in the tank. This "negative split" mindset will serve him well in Phase 3.

---

### Week 7

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 28–32 minutes

**Session 1:** 25 minutes easy continuous jogging. By this point, 25 minutes should be achievable at a genuinely easy pace. If he needs one short 2-minute walk break in the middle, that is acceptable, but encourage him to try without.

**Session 2:** 25 minutes easy continuous jogging. Repeat the same session to build confidence and consistency at this duration.

**Session 3:** 28 minutes easy continuous jogging, or a structured session of 10 minutes / 3-minute walk / 15 minutes if he prefers a break point. The goal is total running volume, not necessarily unbroken continuity yet.

**Coaching focus:** At this stage, begin discussing route planning for outdoor sessions. Encourage him to choose routes that avoid heavy traffic (air pollution can exacerbate EIA), avoid routes that pass through areas with high pollen counts if he has any allergic component to his asthma, and plan routes that allow him to loop back to a start point rather than running point-to-point, so he is never far from shelter or his bag if symptoms arise.

---

### Week 8

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 28–30 minutes

**Session 1:** 28 minutes easy continuous jogging.

**Session 2:** 20 minutes at a slightly brisker pace — RPE 13–14. This is the first session where pace is deliberately increased rather than duration. Keep it controlled and monitor his breathing response carefully.

**Session 3:** 30 minutes easy continuous jogging. This is the longest session to date and marks the end of Phase 2. It should feel manageable — not a maximum effort.

**End-of-Phase 2 Check-In:** Can he run 30 minutes continuously at an easy pace? Is his breathing well-controlled throughout? Has he had any EIA episodes in this phase, and if so, were they managed appropriately? Is he recovering well between sessions — no persistent fatigue, no unusual breathlessness at rest? If all answers are positive, Phase 3 is ready to begin. If there have been recurring EIA episodes, consult with his GP before proceeding and consider whether the pace of progression needs to be adjusted.

---

## Phase 3: Consolidation (Weeks 9–12)
### Goal: Achieve continuous 5K running, build pace confidence, prepare for race-day conditions

Phase 3 shifts the focus from duration to distance and pace. Your client can now run for 30 minutes — the task is to translate that into a confident, comfortable 5K. For most beginners, a 5K at an easy pace takes 35–40 minutes, so the final weeks will push duration slightly beyond 30 minutes while also introducing some gentle pace work to build efficiency.

---

### Week 9

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 30–35 minutes

**Session 1:** 30 minutes easy continuous running. Consolidation run — the goal is comfort and confidence, not pace.

**Session 2:** 30 minutes with a structured middle section. Run 10 minutes easy, then 10 minutes at a slightly brisker pace (RPE 14), then 10 minutes easy to finish. This introduces the concept of pacing variation within a run without the pressure of intervals.

**Session 3:** 35 minutes easy continuous running. This is the first time he will exceed 30 minutes. Pace must be conservative. Remind him that 35 minutes at an easy pace covers approximately 4–4.5 km for most beginners, so he is getting close to 5K territory.

**Coaching focus:** Begin discussing what a 5K race or time trial will look like. Talk through the start-line routine — arriving early enough to warm up properly, pre-treating with the inhaler 15–20 minutes before the gun, wearing appropriate clothing for the weather, and starting at the back of the pack to avoid being swept into a pace that is too fast in the excitement of the event.

---

### Week 10

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 32–38 minutes

**Session 1:** 35 minutes easy continuous running.

**Session 2:** A gentle fartlek session — 30 minutes total, alternating between 3 minutes at easy pace and 1 minute at a comfortably brisk pace (RPE 14–15) throughout. This is not sprint work; the "fast" sections should feel like a purposeful stride, not a race effort. This session builds aerobic efficiency and begins to lower his 5K time without the stress of formal interval training.

**Session 3:** 38 minutes easy continuous running, or run until he reaches 5K — whichever comes first. This is effectively a practice 5K at easy pace. Note the time and distance. This data point is valuable for week 12 planning.

**Coaching focus:** After session 3, debrief thoroughly. How did the near-5K distance feel? Where in the run did he feel strongest and where did he feel it most? Were there any airway symptoms? Use this information to fine-tune the final two weeks.

---

### Week 11

**Sessions per week:** 3 | **Total active time per session:** 30–38 minutes

**Session 1:** 30 minutes easy running. This is a deliberate step back in duration — a recovery session to ensure he arrives at the final week fresh.

**Session 2:** Repeat the fartlek session from week 10, session 2. By now it should feel more natural and controlled.

**Session 3:** 5K at easy, comfortable pace. This is his second practice 5K. The goal is not a time — it is completion with controlled breathing and good form throughout. Celebrate this achievement with him regardless of the time on the clock.

**Coaching focus:** Begin tapering conversation. Explain that week 12 involves reduced volume to ensure he arrives at his goal 5K feeling fresh and confident. Reassure him that reducing mileage in the final week does not mean losing fitness — it means allowing his body to consolidate everything it has built.

---

### Week 12 — The Final Week

**Sessions per week:** 2 running sessions + 1 goal event

**Session 1 (e.g., Monday):** 20–25 minutes easy running. Light, comfortable, confidence-building. No heroics. Focus on smooth breathing and relaxed form.

**Session 2 (e.g., Wednesday):** 15–20 minutes very easy running with 4–5 short 30-second stride-outs (brief accelerations to a comfortable brisk pace, not sprinting) to keep the legs feeling sharp. Finish feeling energised, not tired.

**Goal 5K (e.g., Saturday):** This is the culmination of 12 weeks of work. Whether this is a parkrun, a local race, or a solo time trial on a measured route, the approach is the same.

*Race-day protocol:* Arrive at least 30 minutes before the start. Complete the full 10-minute warm-up routine. Take 2 puffs of the SABA inhaler 15–20 minutes before the start. Dress appropriately for the weather — buff or mask if cold. Start at a conservative pace, slower than feels necessary for the first kilometre. Settle into a comfortable rhythm in kilometres 2 and 3. If he has anything left in kilometres 4 and 5, he can gradually increase effort. Cross the finish line having run the whole distance — that is the only goal.

## Supplementary Strength & Conditioning (Weeks 1–12)

To support his running and reduce injury risk, incorporate two short strength sessions per week on non-running days (e.g., Tuesday and Thursday). These sessions should be 25–30 minutes and kept at low-to-moderate intensity. They are not cardio sessions — keep the heart rate moderate and the breathing comfortable throughout.

**Exercise Selection (perform as a circuit, 2–3 rounds):**

- **Bodyweight squats** — 3 sets of 12–15 reps. Builds quad and glute strength for running economy.
- **Glute bridges** — 3 sets of 15 reps. Activates the posterior chain and protects the lower back.
- **Walking lunges** — 2 sets of 10 each leg. Functional strength and hip flexor mobility.
- **Calf raises** — 3 sets of 15 reps. Protects against Achilles and shin issues common in new runners.
- **Dead bugs** — 2 sets of 8 each side. Core stability without breath-holding or Valsalva manoeuvre — important for an asthmatic client.
- **Resistance band clamshells** — 2 sets of 15 each side. Hip abductor strength to prevent knee tracking issues.
- **Press-ups (modified if needed)** — 2 sets of 8–12 reps. Upper body and core.

**Important note:** Avoid exercises that require prolonged breath-holding or heavy Valsalva manoeuvre (e.g., heavy barbell squats, heavy deadlifts) until you are confident his breathing is well-controlled under load. The dead bug is specifically chosen because it trains core stability while maintaining a breathing rhythm.

---

## Nutrition Guidance

While you haven't specified a detailed nutrition plan, the following principles are relevant for this client and worth communicating.

**Hydration:** Dehydration can thicken airway secretions and worsen EIA symptoms. Encourage consistent daily hydration — approximately 2–2.5 litres of water per day, more on training days. He should arrive at every session already well-hydrated, not trying to catch up during the warm-up.

**Pre-session fuelling:** A light, easily digestible snack 60–90 minutes before running is appropriate — for example, a banana with a small amount of peanut butter, or a small bowl of porridge. Avoid large meals within 2 hours of running, as a full stomach can restrict diaphragm movement and make breathing less efficient.

**Post-session recovery:** Within 30–45 minutes of finishing, encourage a combination of protein and carbohydrate to support muscle repair and glycogen replenishment — for example, a Greek yoghurt with fruit, a chicken and rice bowl, or a protein shake with a piece of fruit. This is particularly important on days when he has both a running session and a strength session.

**Foods that may support respiratory health:** While not a substitute for medication, a diet rich in antioxidants (colourful vegetables and fruits), omega-3 fatty acids (oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed), and vitamin D (oily fish, eggs, fortified foods, or supplementation if deficient) has some evidence of modest benefit for airway inflammation. This is a conversation to have gently and without overstating the evidence.

---

## Recovery & Lifestyle Guidance

**Sleep:** Encourage 7–9 hours per night. Sleep is when the majority of respiratory and muscular repair occurs. Poor sleep is associated with increased airway reactivity in asthmatic individuals.

**Rest days:** The programme includes at least one full rest day between every running session. On rest days, light activity such as walking or gentle yoga is fine and beneficial, but nothing that elevates the heart rate significantly.

**Illness protocol:** If your client develops a respiratory infection — cold, flu, chest infection — running must stop until he has been symptom-free for at least 48–72 hours and his GP is satisfied it is safe to return. Respiratory infections significantly increase EIA risk and can trigger severe bronchospasm. Do not rush back. When returning after illness, drop back two weeks in the programme and rebuild gradually.

**Pollen and air quality:** On high-pollen days (particularly in spring and early summer) or days with poor air quality ratings, consider moving outdoor sessions indoors. Many weather apps now include pollen and air quality indices. Encourage your client to check these as part of his pre-session routine.

**Ongoing GP communication:** Recommend that your client has a brief check-in with his GP at the 6-week mark and again at the end of the 12 weeks. This keeps his medical team informed of his progress, allows for any medication review if needed, and ensures that his asthma management plan remains appropriate as his fitness level changes.

# Strength Training Programme — 12-Week Addition
### Integrated with the Couch-to-5K Plan

## Programming Philosophy for This Client

Before laying out the sessions, it is worth explaining the thinking behind the exercise selection and structure, because several decisions are directly shaped by his asthma.

**Why strength training helps an asthmatic runner:** Stronger legs mean better running economy — he achieves the same pace with less cardiovascular effort, which means less ventilatory demand and a lower EIA trigger threshold. A strong posterior chain reduces compensatory breathing patterns caused by poor posture. Core stability allows him to maintain an upright, open chest position throughout a run, keeping the airways as unobstructed as possible. These are not incidental benefits — they are directly relevant to his condition.

**What to avoid and why:** Heavy compound lifts performed at maximal or near-maximal loads require prolonged Valsalva manoeuvre — a forceful breath-hold against a closed glottis that dramatically increases intrathoracic pressure. For an asthmatic client, this can trigger bronchospasm and is unnecessary at this stage of his training. All loading in this programme stays in a range where he can maintain a continuous breathing rhythm throughout every repetition. He should never hold his breath during any exercise. Cue this actively and consistently.

**Breathing cue for every exercise:** Exhale on the effort (the hardest part of the movement), inhale on the return. For example, exhale as he stands from a squat, inhale as he lowers. This is standard resistance training breathing practice, but for this client it is a clinical priority, not just good form.

**Session structure:** Two dedicated strength sessions per week, placed on non-running days. The suggested layout across the full week is as follows.

| Day | Activity |
|---|---|
| Monday | Run session |
| Tuesday | Strength session A |
| Wednesday | Run session |
| Thursday | Strength session B |
| Friday | Rest or light walk / mobility |
| Saturday | Run session |
| Sunday | Full rest |

This layout ensures no two demanding sessions fall back-to-back and gives his respiratory system adequate recovery between running efforts. If life requires a different arrangement, the firm rule is simply this: never schedule a strength session immediately after a hard run session, and always keep at least one full rest day somewhere in the week.

**Session duration:** 35–45 minutes including warm-up and cool-down. These are not long sessions. Quality of movement and breathing control matter far more than volume at this stage.

**Warm-up for strength sessions:** 5 minutes of light movement — arm circles, leg swings, hip circles, bodyweight squats with a pause at the bottom, and cat-cow breathing on all fours. The cat-cow specifically is valuable for this client as it links spinal movement to breath and helps open the chest before loading. Finish with 10 slow, deliberate diaphragmatic breaths — inhale through the nose for 4 counts, exhale through pursed lips for 6 counts. This activates the diaphragm, calms the nervous system, and prepares the airways.

**Cool-down for strength sessions:** 5 minutes of static stretching — hip flexors, chest opener, thoracic rotation, and hamstrings. Finish with another round of diaphragmatic breathing. Keeping the cool-down consistent across both running and strength sessions reinforces the habit and ensures his airways always return to baseline gradually.

## Phase Structure

The strength programme mirrors the three phases of the running plan and progresses in a logical, manageable way.

| Phase | Weeks | Strength Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | 1–4 | Movement quality, bodyweight foundations, breathing control |
| Phase 2 | 5–8 | Load introduction, unilateral work, running-specific strength |
| Phase 3 | 9–12 | Power endurance, race-specific conditioning, taper |

## Phase 1: Movement Foundations (Weeks 1–4)

### Goal: Establish correct movement patterns, build postural strength, embed breathing discipline under load

Everything in Phase 1 is bodyweight or very light resistance. Do not be tempted to add load early. Your client needs to learn how to breathe through effort before he learns how to lift. A client who can squat 80 kg but holds his breath throughout every rep is a higher-risk client than one who can squat 40 kg with perfect breathing rhythm. Establish the rhythm first.

---

### Session A — Lower Body and Core Focus

Perform as a straight-set format (complete all sets of one exercise before moving to the next) rather than a circuit in Phase 1. This gives more recovery time between sets and makes it easier to monitor breathing between efforts.

**1. Bodyweight Squat**
3 sets of 12 reps. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. Inhale on the way down, exhale on the way up. Pause for one second at the bottom of each rep to reinforce depth and control. Rest 60–90 seconds between sets. Coaching cue: chest tall, knees tracking over toes, weight through the whole foot. This is the foundation of every lower-body pattern in the programme.

**2. Glute Bridge**
3 sets of 15 reps. Lying on his back, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Exhale as he drives the hips up, inhale as he lowers. Hold the top position for 2 seconds on each rep. Rest 60 seconds between sets. This is one of the most important exercises in the programme for a runner — it activates the gluteus maximus, which is chronically underused in sedentary individuals and essential for propulsion and knee stability in running.

**3. Dead Bug**
3 sets of 6 reps each side. Lying on his back, arms pointing to the ceiling, knees bent at 90 degrees in the air. Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg toward the floor while exhaling, return while inhaling. The lower back must stay in contact with the floor throughout. Rest 60 seconds between sets. This exercise is specifically chosen because it builds deep core stability while demanding continuous, controlled breathing — it is almost impossible to do correctly while holding your breath, which makes it an excellent training tool for this client.

**4. Calf Raise**
3 sets of 15 reps. Standing on a step or flat floor, rise onto the balls of both feet, lower slowly over 3 seconds. Breathe freely and continuously throughout. Rest 45 seconds between sets. Calf strength is frequently neglected in beginner runners and is one of the primary contributors to shin splints and Achilles tendinopathy — both common in this population.

**5. Resistance Band Clamshell**
2 sets of 15 reps each side. Light resistance band just above the knees. Lying on his side, hips stacked, knees bent. Open the top knee like a clamshell while keeping the feet together. Exhale on the open, inhale on the close. Rest 45 seconds between sides. This targets the gluteus medius, which controls hip abduction and prevents the knee from collapsing inward during running — a major cause of runner's knee in beginners.

**6. Diaphragmatic Breathing Finish**
Not an exercise in the traditional sense, but end every Session A with 2 minutes of deliberate diaphragmatic breathing. Lying on his back, one hand on the chest and one on the belly. Breathe so that only the belly hand rises. Inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6. This is both a recovery tool and a respiratory training technique. Diaphragmatic breathing strengthens the primary breathing muscle and can reduce the work of accessory breathing muscles that become overactive in asthmatic individuals.

---

### Session B — Upper Body, Posture, and Core Focus

**1. Press-Up (modified or full)**
3 sets of 8–10 reps. If full press-ups are not yet achievable with good form, begin from the knees. Exhale on the push, inhale on the lower. Lower slowly over 2–3 seconds. Rest 60–90 seconds between sets. Upper body pressing strength supports the arm drive that contributes to running economy and helps maintain an upright posture under fatigue.

**2. Dumbbell Row (single arm, supported on bench)**
3 sets of 10 reps each side. Light dumbbell — start at a weight where the last 2 reps are mildly challenging but form is perfect. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the lower. Rest 60 seconds between sides. Rowing movements counterbalance the forward-rounded posture that many sedentary individuals bring to a running programme and that worsens under fatigue. An open chest is a more efficient breathing chest.

**3. Dumbbell Shoulder Press (seated)**
2 sets of 10 reps. Light dumbbells. Seated with back supported. Exhale as he presses overhead, inhale as he lowers. Rest 60–90 seconds between sets. Overhead pressing builds shoulder stability and reinforces the upright posture needed for efficient running breathing mechanics.

**4. Walking Lunge**
2 sets of 10 reps each leg. Bodyweight only. Exhale on the step and lower, inhale on the return to standing. Focus on a long stride and upright torso. Rest 60 seconds between sets. The walking lunge builds unilateral leg strength and hip flexor mobility simultaneously — both directly relevant to running.

**5. Plank**
3 sets, building duration across the phase. Week 1: 20 seconds. Week 2: 25 seconds. Week 3: 30 seconds. Week 4: 35 seconds. Breathing must be continuous throughout — slow, steady nasal breathing if possible. If he holds his breath at any point, reduce the duration. Rest 45–60 seconds between sets. The plank builds anterior core stiffness that translates directly to running posture and reduces energy leakage through the trunk.

**6. Thoracic Rotation Stretch (active)**
2 sets of 8 reps each side. Seated on the floor or a bench, hands behind the head, rotate the upper back to each side. Inhale to prepare, exhale into the rotation. This is both a mobility exercise and a breathing exercise — thoracic rotation is closely linked to rib cage expansion and respiratory capacity. Many asthmatic individuals develop a stiff thoracic spine from habitually guarded breathing patterns, and this exercise directly addresses that.

---

### Phase 1 Progression Notes

Across weeks 1–4, the exercises remain the same but the following small progressions apply. In week 2, add one additional set to the squat and glute bridge (moving from 3 to 4 sets). In week 3, increase the press-up and row reps by 2 (so 10–12 reps). In week 4, perform the bodyweight squat with a 3-second lowering tempo to increase time under tension without adding load. These are small, deliberate steps. The goal is not to exhaust him — it is to build a movement vocabulary he can carry into Phase 2.

## Phase 2: Load Introduction (Weeks 5–8)

### Goal: Introduce external load, develop unilateral strength, build running-specific power endurance

Phase 2 introduces dumbbells and a resistance band into the lower body work, and increases the challenge of the core exercises. The breathing discipline established in Phase 1 is now tested under load — this is where your coaching eye is most important. Watch for breath-holding, particularly during the goblet squat and Romanian deadlift. If you see it, reduce the load immediately.

The format shifts slightly in Phase 2. Sessions are now performed as paired supersets — two exercises performed back-to-back with a short rest between pairs. This increases the metabolic demand modestly and better reflects the sustained effort of running, while keeping the session time manageable.

---

### Session A — Lower Body and Core (Phase 2)

**Superset 1: Goblet Squat + Dead Bug**
Perform the goblet squat, rest 30 seconds, perform the dead bug, rest 60 seconds, then repeat.

*Goblet Squat:* 3 sets of 10 reps. Hold a single dumbbell vertically at the chest. Start with a weight that feels manageable — 8–10 kg is a reasonable starting point for most beginners, but adjust based on your assessment. Exhale on the ascent, inhale on the descent. The goblet position naturally encourages an upright torso, which is ideal for this client as it keeps the chest open and breathing unobstructed.

*Dead Bug:* 3 sets of 8 reps each side. Same technique as Phase 1 but with a slower tempo — take 3 seconds to lower the arm and leg, 2 seconds to return. The increased time under tension makes this significantly more challenging without any additional load.

**Superset 2: Romanian Deadlift + Resistance Band Clamshell**

*Romanian Deadlift (RDL):* 3 sets of 10 reps. Two dumbbells, starting at 8–12 kg each depending on his strength. Hinge at the hips, maintaining a neutral spine, lowering the dumbbells along the front of the legs until a hamstring stretch is felt, then drive the hips forward to return. Exhale on the return, inhale on the hinge. This is the most technically demanding exercise introduced so far — spend time on the hip hinge pattern before adding load. A strong posterior chain is the single biggest contributor to running economy and injury prevention.

*Resistance Band Clamshell:* 3 sets of 15 reps each side. Move to a medium resistance band if the light band has become easy. Same technique as Phase 1.

**Superset 3: Step-Up + Calf Raise**

*Step-Up:* 3 sets of 10 reps each leg. Using a sturdy bench or box at approximately knee height. Step up leading with one leg, drive through the heel, bring the trailing leg up to standing, then step back down with control. Add light dumbbells (5–8 kg each hand) from week 6 onwards if bodyweight feels easy. Exhale on the step up, inhale on the step down. Step-ups are highly specific to running mechanics and build single-leg strength and balance simultaneously.

*Calf Raise (single leg):* 3 sets of 12 reps each leg. Progress from the bilateral calf raise of Phase 1 to a single-leg version. Hold a light dumbbell in the same-side hand for added load from week 7. This progression is important — running is a single-leg activity, and the calf must be strong enough to absorb and generate force on one leg at a time.

**Finisher: Pallof Press**
2 sets of 10 reps each side. Using a resistance band anchored to a fixed point at chest height, or a cable machine if available. Stand side-on to the anchor point, hold the band at the chest, press it straight out in front and return. The band will try to rotate the torso — resist it. Exhale on the press, inhale on the return. This is an anti-rotation core exercise that builds the lateral core stability needed to prevent excessive trunk rotation during running, which is a common energy waster and injury contributor in beginners.

---

### Session B — Upper Body, Posture, and Core (Phase 2)

**Superset 1: Dumbbell Bench Press + Bent-Over Dumbbell Row**

*Dumbbell Bench Press:* 3 sets of 10 reps. Lying on a bench, dumbbells at chest height, press to full extension. Exhale on the press, inhale on the lower. A 2-second lowering tempo. This replaces the press-up as the primary horizontal push exercise now that a baseline of upper body strength has been established.

*Bent-Over Dumbbell Row (bilateral):* 3 sets of 10 reps. Hinge forward at the hips to approximately 45 degrees, dumbbells hanging, row both to the hips simultaneously. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the lower. The bilateral version increases the postural demand on the lower back and core compared to the supported single-arm row of Phase 1.

**Superset 2: Dumbbell Shoulder Press + Face Pull (band)**

*Dumbbell Shoulder Press (standing):* 3 sets of 10 reps. Progress from seated to standing, which increases core demand. Exhale on the press, inhale on the lower. Keep the ribcage down — avoid flaring the ribs upward as this compresses the lower back and restricts diaphragm movement.

*Face Pull (resistance band):* 3 sets of 15 reps. Band anchored at face height. Pull the band toward the face, separating the hands as they approach, finishing with the hands beside the ears and elbows high. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return. Face pulls are one of the most effective exercises for shoulder health and thoracic posture — they strengthen the external rotators and rear deltoids that are chronically weak in people who sit at desks, and they directly counteract the forward-rounded shoulder posture that restricts breathing capacity.

**Superset 3: Walking Lunge + Plank Variation**

*Walking Lunge with Dumbbells:* 3 sets of 12 reps each leg. Add light dumbbells (5–8 kg each hand) from week 5. Maintain an upright torso throughout. Exhale on the step and lower, inhale on the return.

*Plank with Shoulder Tap:* 3 sets of 8 taps each side. From a full plank position, lift one hand to tap the opposite shoulder, replacing it before lifting the other. The goal is to resist rotation — the hips should stay level throughout. Breathe continuously. This is a significant progression from the static plank and directly trains the anti-rotation core stability needed in running.

**Finisher: Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller**
This is a mobility and respiratory exercise combined. Place a foam roller perpendicular to the spine at mid-back level. Support the head with the hands. Gently extend over the roller, opening the chest toward the ceiling. Hold for 3–5 slow breaths, then move the roller one segment up the spine and repeat. Work through 4–5 positions from mid-back to upper back. This directly addresses thoracic stiffness, opens the anterior chest, and improves rib cage expansion — all of which increase breathing efficiency. Spend 3–4 minutes on this at the end of every Session B in Phase 2.

### Phase 2 Progression Notes

In weeks 5 and 6, focus on technique with the new loaded exercises before increasing weight. In weeks 7 and 8, increase the dumbbell load by 2 kg on the goblet squat, RDL, and bench press if form is solid and breathing is controlled. Never increase load and volume simultaneously — if you add weight, keep the reps the same. The step-up and single-leg calf raise should also receive a small load increase in week 8 if week 7 felt comfortable.

## Phase 3: Power Endurance and Race Preparation (Weeks 9–12)

### Goal: Build muscular endurance specific to 5K running, introduce light plyometric work, taper appropriately in week 12

Phase 3 introduces two new elements. First, the rep ranges shift upward in some exercises to build muscular endurance — the ability of the muscles to sustain repeated contractions over the duration of a 5K, which is more relevant than maximal strength for this goal. Second, very light plyometric work is introduced in the form of low-impact jumping and bounding. Plyometrics improve running economy by training the stretch-shortening cycle — the elastic recoil of the tendons and muscles that makes running more efficient. For an asthmatic client, plyometrics must be introduced carefully, as the increased ventilatory demand of explosive work can trigger EIA. Start conservatively, monitor his response, and progress only if he remains symptom-free.

### Session A — Lower Body, Core, and Plyometrics (Phase 3)

**1. Goblet Squat**
4 sets of 12 reps. Increase load by 2–4 kg from Phase 2 if form and breathing are solid. Same technique and breathing cues as before.

**2. Romanian Deadlift**
4 sets of 10 reps. Increase load modestly from Phase 2. Focus on a controlled 3-second lowering phase to maximise hamstring loading.

**3. Bulgarian Split Squat**
3 sets of 8 reps each leg. Rear foot elevated on a bench, front foot forward. Lower the back knee toward the floor, keeping the front shin as vertical as possible. Bodyweight only in week 9, add light dumbbells (5–6 kg each hand) from week 10 if comfortable. Exhale on the ascent, inhale on the descent. This is the most demanding lower body exercise in the programme and directly replicates the single-leg loading of running. It will feel challenging — reassure him that this is normal and that the difficulty is the point.

**4. Box Jump (low impact introduction)**
2 sets of 6 reps. Weeks 9–10 only. Use a low box or step (20–30 cm). Step up onto the box with both feet, then step back down — do not jump yet. This is a loaded step-up with a focus on the landing mechanics. In weeks 11–12, if he has been completely symptom-free during all Phase 3 sessions, progress to a two-foot jump onto the box with a soft, controlled landing. Land quietly — loud landings indicate poor absorption and increase injury risk. If there is any airway response to this exercise, remove it from the programme immediately and return to step-ups. Monitor his breathing for 5 minutes after this exercise specifically.

**5. Single-Leg Glute Bridge**
3 sets of 12 reps each leg. Progress from the bilateral glute bridge of Phase 1. Same technique but one foot lifted off the floor. Exhale on the drive, inhale on the lower.

**6. Dead Bug with Dumbbell**
3 sets of 8 reps each side. Hold a light dumbbell (2–4 kg) in the hand of the extending arm. The added load increases the demand on the deep core without compromising the breathing pattern. If breathing becomes disrupted, remove the dumbbell.

### Session B — Upper Body, Posture, and Endurance (Phase 3)

**1. Dumbbell Bench Press**
4 sets of 12 reps. Slightly lighter than the Phase 2 load to accommodate the higher rep range. The goal is muscular endurance, not maximal strength.

**2. Bent-Over Dumbbell Row**
4 sets of 12 reps. Same principle — slightly lighter load, higher reps, continuous breathing throughout.

**3. Dumbbell Lateral Raise**
3 sets of 15 reps. Light dumbbells. Raise the arms to shoulder height, lower slowly over 3 seconds. Exhale on the raise, inhale on the lower. Builds shoulder endurance and reinforces the arm carriage position used in running.

**4. Resistance Band Pull-Apart**
3 sets of 20 reps. Hold a light resistance band at chest height with straight arms, pull it apart until the arms are wide, return slowly. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return. This is a high-rep postural endurance exercise that directly trains the muscles responsible for keeping the chest open and the shoulders back during the later stages of a run when fatigue sets in and posture collapses.

**5. Reverse Lunge with Rotation**
3 sets of 10 reps each leg. Step back into a reverse lunge, and at the bottom of the lunge, rotate the torso toward the front leg. Return to standing. Bodyweight only. Exhale on the rotation, inhale on the return to standing. This combines hip strength, balance, and thoracic rotation — all relevant to running mechanics — in a single movement.

**6. Plank to Down Dog**
3 sets of 8 reps. From a full plank position, push the hips up and back into a downward dog position, then return to plank. Exhale into the down dog, inhale back to plank. This dynamic movement builds shoulder stability, hamstring flexibility, and thoracic mobility simultaneously, and the breathing pattern is built into the movement itself.

**7. Foam Roller Thoracic Extension**
Continue from Phase 2. 3–4 minutes at the end of every Session B. By Phase 3, this should feel noticeably more comfortable than it did in week 5, reflecting genuine improvement in thoracic mobility.

The goal is to maintain neuromuscular activation and keep the legs feeling sharp without accumulating any fatigue before the goal 5K on Saturday. Do not introduce any new exercises, do not test maximal effort, and keep the session to 30 minutes maximum. Session B is dropped entirely in week 12.

## Programming Philosophy for Pace Work in an Asthmatic Client

Before laying out the sessions, it is important to be transparent about why pace work requires particular care with this client and how the structure below manages that risk without eliminating the stimulus entirely.

High-intensity running is the single biggest trigger for exercise-induced asthma. The faster the pace, the greater the ventilatory demand, the more air moves through the airways per minute, and the greater the drying and cooling effect on the bronchial mucosa that drives bronchospasm. This does not mean your client cannot run fast — it means fast running must be introduced progressively, preceded by a thorough warm-up, and monitored carefully. Many elite athletes with EIA compete at world-class level. The difference between them and an unmanaged asthmatic is preparation and discipline, not physiology.

The approach taken here is to introduce pace work in three stages. In weeks 7 and 8, the stimulus is gentle — controlled stride-outs and relaxed tempo efforts that lift the heart rate without approaching maximal ventilation. In weeks 9 and 10, structured tempo running and short intervals appear, with walk or easy jog recoveries that allow the airways to recover between efforts. In weeks 11 and 12, the pace work becomes race-specific — efforts at or slightly above goal 5K pace that prepare both the body and the mind for the demands of the event.

Throughout all pace work, the pre-exercise inhaler protocol remains mandatory. On days when a pace session is planned, your client should be especially diligent about this. If he has had any respiratory symptoms in the 24 hours before a planned pace session — unusual breathlessness, chest tightness, a cold beginning — downgrade the session to an easy run. No pace session is worth triggering a significant EIA episode.

One additional note on warm-up for pace sessions specifically. The standard 10-minute warm-up described in the original programme is the minimum for easy running days. On pace session days, extend the warm-up to **15 minutes minimum**, and include 4–6 progressive stride-outs at the end of the warm-up before the first hard effort begins. These stride-outs — 20-second accelerations to a brisk but controlled pace with full recovery between each — serve a specific physiological purpose. There is good evidence that a series of short, high-intensity efforts performed during the warm-up can induce a refractory period of up to 2–3 hours during which EIA severity is significantly reduced. This is sometimes called the refractory period warm-up strategy and it is one of the most effective non-pharmacological tools available for this client. Use it every single time before pace work.

---

## Pace Terminology Used in This Programme

To avoid ambiguity, the following definitions apply throughout.

**Easy pace:** Fully conversational. Could hold a long conversation without effort. RPE 11–12. This is the pace used for all base running in weeks 1–6 and for warm-up and cool-down running in all subsequent weeks.

**Comfortable tempo pace:** Can speak in short sentences but would not choose to hold a conversation. Breathing is noticeably elevated but controlled and rhythmic. RPE 13–14. This is the primary pace development tool in weeks 7–9.

**Strong tempo pace:** Speaking is possible only in single words or very short phrases. Breathing is working hard. RPE 15–16. Used in weeks 10–12 for shorter efforts.

**5K race pace:** The pace he intends to run his goal 5K at. Based on his progress through the programme, a realistic target for a 24-year-old completing this programme is somewhere between 28 and 35 minutes for 5K, depending on his natural aerobic capacity. His race pace is therefore approximately 5:36–7:00 per kilometre. You will have a clearer picture of where he sits by week 8 based on his easy-pace running times. A useful rule of thumb is that comfortable tempo pace should feel roughly 45–60 seconds per kilometre faster than his easy pace, and strong tempo pace roughly 30–45 seconds per kilometre faster than comfortable tempo.

---

## Revised Running Sessions: Weeks 7–12

The strength programme remains as previously described. What follows replaces or modifies the running sessions from week 7 onwards. Weeks 1–6 remain unchanged from the original plan.

---

### Week 7 — Introduction to Controlled Pace Variation

This week introduces the concept of running at different speeds within a single session. The efforts are gentle and the primary goal is simply to teach your client that he can run faster than easy pace without his airways immediately rebelling, provided the warm-up has been done properly and the effort is controlled.

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Continuous Run**
25 minutes at easy pace. No pace work. This session exists to consolidate the continuous running achieved at the end of week 6 and to give him a confident, comfortable run before the pace introduction later in the week. RPE 11–12 throughout.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — Stride-Out Introduction**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 4 progressive stride-outs as described above. Then run 20 minutes easy, but every 5 minutes, insert a 30-second acceleration to comfortable tempo pace before returning to easy pace. So the structure is: 5 minutes easy, 30 seconds tempo, 5 minutes easy, 30 seconds tempo, and so on for four cycles. Cool down with 8 minutes of easy walking and stretching. The tempo efforts are short enough that airway response should be minimal, but monitor him closely during and for 10 minutes after the session. Ask him to rate his breathing on a simple 1–5 scale after each tempo effort (1 = completely fine, 5 = significant tightness). If he scores 3 or above on any effort, bring the session back to easy pace for the remainder.

**Session 3 (Saturday) — Extended Easy Run with Finish Surge**
28 minutes easy, then in the final 2 minutes, gradually increase pace to comfortable tempo and hold it to the finish. This is not a sprint finish — it is a controlled, progressive increase that teaches him to lift pace when fatigued, which is a specific skill needed in the final kilometre of a 5K. Cool down thoroughly.

---

### Week 8 — Building Tempo Confidence

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Continuous Run**
30 minutes easy. Consolidation and recovery from the pace work introduced in week 7. RPE 11–12.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — First Structured Tempo Blocks**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 5 stride-outs. Then: 5 minutes easy running, followed by 3 minutes at comfortable tempo pace, followed by 3 minutes easy recovery running, followed by 3 minutes at comfortable tempo pace, followed by 3 minutes easy recovery, followed by 3 minutes at comfortable tempo pace. Finish with 5 minutes easy and a full cool-down. Total tempo volume: 9 minutes across three blocks. This is the most demanding running session to date. Pace the first tempo block conservatively — it is very common for beginners to go out too hard on the first interval and struggle on the subsequent ones. The third block should feel no harder than the first.

**Session 3 (Saturday) — Longer Easy Run**
32–35 minutes easy. The purpose of this session is aerobic volume, not pace. After the intensity of Wednesday, the body needs a longer, easier effort to consolidate the aerobic adaptations being driven by the tempo work. Do not be tempted to add pace work here.

**End-of-Week 8 Assessment:** After this week, you should have a clear picture of how his airways respond to sustained tempo efforts. If the three-minute tempo blocks in session 2 produced any significant airway symptoms, do not progress to the harder pace work in weeks 9 and 10 until you have consulted his GP and confirmed that his SABA management is adequate for the increased intensity. If he sailed through with minimal symptoms, proceed with confidence.

---

### Week 9 — Tempo Running Established

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Run**
30 minutes easy. Active recovery from the previous week's tempo work.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — Extended Tempo Session**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 5–6 stride-outs. Then: 2 minutes easy, 5 minutes at comfortable tempo pace, 3 minutes easy recovery, 5 minutes at comfortable tempo pace, 3 minutes easy recovery, 5 minutes at comfortable tempo pace, 2 minutes easy. Cool down fully. Total tempo volume: 15 minutes across three blocks. The individual blocks are now 5 minutes long, which is a meaningful step up from the 3-minute blocks of week 8. The pace should be the same — comfortable tempo, RPE 13–14. If he finds himself working harder than RPE 14 to maintain the pace, he is running too fast. Slow down rather than shorten the interval.

**Session 3 (Saturday) — Progression Run**
This is a new session type. Start at easy pace and every 8 minutes, lift the pace by a small, controlled increment. The structure is: 8 minutes easy, 8 minutes comfortable tempo, 8 minutes strong tempo, 3 minutes easy cool-down running. Total: approximately 27 minutes of running. This session teaches him to run through three distinct gears and to manage his breathing as the demand increases. The strong tempo section at the end — RPE 15–16 — is the hardest running he will have done in the programme so far. It will be uncomfortable. Coach him through it by reminding him to focus on his breathing rhythm rather than the discomfort, to keep his shoulders relaxed and his arms driving, and to know that the 8 minutes has a defined end point.

---

### Week 10 — Introducing Short Intervals

Week 10 introduces interval training for the first time. Intervals — repeated efforts at a hard pace with recovery periods between them — are the most effective tool for improving running speed and aerobic capacity, but they are also the highest-risk session type for EIA. The intervals used here are deliberately short (90 seconds to 2 minutes) and the recovery periods are generous (equal to or greater than the effort duration) to ensure his airways have time to recover between efforts. The refractory period warm-up is especially important this week.

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Run**
30 minutes easy. Do not add any pace work to this session. The interval session on Wednesday needs him arriving fresh.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — First Interval Session**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 6 progressive stride-outs, with the final two stride-outs reaching strong tempo pace briefly. Rest 2 minutes after the warm-up before beginning the intervals. Then: 6 repetitions of 90 seconds at strong tempo pace (RPE 15–16) with 2 minutes of easy jogging recovery between each. After the final interval, jog easily for 5 minutes and cool down fully. Total hard effort: 9 minutes across six repetitions. Between each interval, use the recovery jog to consciously slow and deepen the breathing — in through the nose for 3–4 steps, out through the mouth for 4–5 steps. This active recovery breathing helps clear the airways and reduces the risk of cumulative bronchospasm across the session. Monitor his breathing score after each interval. If it reaches 3 or above on the 1–5 scale, extend the recovery to 3 minutes before the next effort. If it reaches 4 or above, end the interval portion of the session and finish with easy jogging only.

**Session 3 (Saturday) — Tempo Continuous Run**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 4 stride-outs. Then run 20 minutes at a steady comfortable tempo pace — not intervals, not a progression, just a sustained 20-minute effort at RPE 13–14. This is sometimes called a threshold run and it is one of the most powerful sessions for improving 5K performance. The 20-minute duration at this intensity is challenging but achievable given the base he has built. Finish with a full cool-down. Note his approximate pace for this session — it will be a useful reference point for setting his 5K race pace target in weeks 11 and 12.

---

### Week 11 — Race-Specific Preparation

Week 11 is the hardest week of the programme. The sessions are designed to simulate the demands of a 5K race and to give him the confidence of knowing he has already run at race pace before the event itself.

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Run**
25 minutes easy. Shorter than recent Monday sessions — this is deliberate. The two harder sessions later in the week need him arriving with fresh legs.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — Race-Pace Intervals**
Warm up for 15 minutes including 6 stride-outs, the last two reaching race pace briefly. Then: 5 repetitions of 3 minutes at 5K race pace with 90 seconds of easy jogging recovery between each. After the final interval, jog easily for 5 minutes and cool down fully. Total race-pace effort: 15 minutes. This session is the closest simulation of 5K race conditions in the entire programme. The 3-minute intervals at race pace with short recoveries replicate the sustained intensity of the event. He will find this hard. Remind him that the discomfort is temporary, that his breathing is controlled, and that he has done the work to be ready for this. If he completes all five intervals at race pace with controlled breathing, he is ready for his goal 5K.

**Session 3 (Saturday) — Practice 5K Time Trial**
This is a full 5K run at his best controlled effort — not an all-out sprint, but a genuine attempt to run the distance at a pace he can sustain from start to finish. Use the full 15-minute warm-up with stride-outs. Pre-treat with the inhaler 15–20 minutes before starting. Run the first kilometre at comfortable tempo pace — slightly slower than he thinks he needs to go. Settle into race pace from kilometre 2. If he feels strong at kilometre 4, he can begin to push. Record the time. This is his benchmark and his dress rehearsal. Celebrate the completion regardless of the time — finishing a 5K time trial in week 11 of a couch-to-5K programme is a genuine achievement. Debrief thoroughly on pacing, breathing, and how he felt at each kilometre marker. Use this information to plan his race-day pacing strategy for week 12.

---

### Week 12 — Taper and Goal Event

The taper week is not a rest week — it is a precision week. The volume drops significantly but the intensity is maintained in short doses to keep the neuromuscular system sharp and prevent the flat, heavy-legged feeling that comes from complete rest before a race.

**Session 1 (Monday) — Easy Run with Strides**
20 minutes easy running, then 4 × 20-second stride-outs at race pace with full recovery between each. The stride-outs keep the legs feeling quick without accumulating fatigue. Finish with a full cool-down. Total session time approximately 35 minutes including warm-up and cool-down.

**Session 2 (Wednesday) — Short Sharpener**
10 minutes easy running, then 3 × 60 seconds at race pace with 2 minutes easy jogging recovery, then 10 minutes easy. This session should leave him feeling energised, not tired. If he feels flat or heavy during the race-pace efforts, it is likely residual fatigue from week 11 — reduce the efforts to 3 × 30 seconds and keep everything else easy. Do not add any additional running this week beyond these two sessions.

**Goal 5K (Saturday) — Race Day**

The race-day protocol deserves detailed attention because for an asthmatic client, the environment and preparation on the day are as important as the fitness he has built.

*The day before:* Normal eating and hydration. No alcohol. Lay out his kit including the inhaler — check it has sufficient doses remaining. If the forecast shows cold temperatures (below 10°C), prepare the buff or face mask. Get a good night's sleep, but do not stress if pre-race nerves make this difficult — one poor night's sleep has minimal impact on performance.

*Race morning:* A light, familiar breakfast 2–3 hours before the start — nothing new, nothing heavy. Continue hydrating normally. Arrive at the venue at least 40 minutes before the start time to allow for registration, a proper warm-up, and time to settle.

*Warm-up (30 minutes before start):* Complete the full 15-minute warm-up routine including 6 progressive stride-outs, with the final two reaching race pace. This is the refractory period warm-up — it is not optional on race day. Take 2 puffs of the SABA inhaler exactly 15–20 minutes before the race start, after the warm-up is complete. Keep the inhaler accessible — in a running belt or handed to you as the trainer at the finish line.

*The race:* Start conservatively. In the excitement of a race environment, it is extremely common for beginners to go out 20–30 seconds per kilometre faster than intended in the first kilometre. This is particularly dangerous for an asthmatic client because a too-fast start drives ventilation up sharply before the airways have fully adapted to the effort, significantly increasing bronchospasm risk. Coach him to start at the back of the pack, run his own race, and trust the pacing strategy you have rehearsed. Kilometre 1 should feel almost too easy. Kilometres 2 and 3 are the engine room — settle into race pace and hold it. Kilometre 4 is where he will begin to feel the effort — focus on breathing rhythm and form, not pace. Kilometre 5 — if he has anything left, use it. Cross the line.

*After the race:* Do not stop abruptly at the finish line. Keep walking for at least 5 minutes. Complete the full cool-down stretching routine. Monitor his breathing for 15–20 minutes post-finish — late-phase bronchospasm can occur 4–8 hours after exercise in some asthmatic individuals, so advise him to be aware of any chest tightness developing later in the day and to use his inhaler if needed.

## A Note on Managing Ambition

Your client is 24 years old, and once he discovers he can run faster, he will want to run faster still. This is a good instinct and should be encouraged — but channelled carefully. The structure above gives him a clear progression that respects his condition while genuinely pushing his pace. The most important thing you can communicate to him as he moves through weeks 9–12 is that the easy days must stay easy. The common mistake among improving runners is turning every session into a moderate effort — working too hard on recovery days and arriving at the hard sessions already fatigued. For an asthmatic client, this is doubly problematic because accumulated fatigue increases airway reactivity. Protect the easy days fiercely. The hard sessions will then deliver everything they are designed to deliver.

# Interval Training Programme
### Structured Speed Development for an Asthmatic Runner

---

## Preamble: Intervals and EIA — The Full Picture

Before laying out the sessions, it is worth being direct about what interval training means for this specific client, because the conversation you have with him before beginning this phase will shape how safely and effectively he executes it.

Interval training is the most powerful tool available for improving running speed and aerobic capacity. It is also, unambiguously, the highest-risk training modality for exercise-induced asthma. The reason is straightforward. During high-intensity intervals, minute ventilation — the total volume of air moving through the airways per minute — can reach 100–150 litres per minute compared to perhaps 15–20 litres at rest. This massive increase in airflow dramatically amplifies the drying and cooling of the bronchial mucosa that drives EIA bronchospasm. The risk is not theoretical. Poorly managed interval training in an asthmatic athlete can trigger severe bronchospasm that requires emergency intervention.

However, the evidence is equally clear that well-managed interval training in controlled asthmatic athletes is not only safe but beneficial. Regular aerobic training reduces baseline airway inflammation, improves cardiovascular efficiency so that the same pace requires less ventilatory effort, and raises the intensity threshold at which EIA is triggered. The goal of this programme is to capture those benefits while managing the risks systematically.

Three principles govern every decision in this interval programme. First, progression is non-negotiable — effort duration, intensity, and volume increase gradually across the weeks, never in large jumps. Second, the refractory period warm-up is used before every interval session without exception. Third, your client must have a clear, rehearsed response plan for every session — he knows what to do if symptoms develop, and so do you.

---

## Prerequisites Before Beginning This Programme

This interval programme is designed to follow the 12-week couch-to-5K plan already completed. Before starting, confirm the following.

Your client can run 5K continuously at a comfortable pace. His EIA is well-controlled on his current SABA regimen with no significant breakthrough symptoms during the couch-to-5K programme. He has a current, reviewed asthma action plan from his GP that specifically addresses exercise. His inhaler technique has been checked — poor inhaler technique is surprisingly common and dramatically reduces drug delivery. If there is any doubt, refer him back to his GP or asthma nurse for a technique review before beginning. He understands and can independently execute the refractory period warm-up. He owns and consistently uses a buff or cold-air mask for outdoor sessions in cold weather.

If any of these prerequisites are not met, address them before the first interval session. There is no urgency that justifies skipping this checklist.

---

## Programme Structure Overview

The interval programme runs for 12 weeks and is divided into four phases of three weeks each. Each phase introduces a new interval format or intensity level, building systematically on the previous phase.

| Phase | Weeks | Interval Type | Primary Stimulus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | 1–3 | Short aerobic intervals | Aerobic capacity, airway adaptation |
| Phase 2 | 4–6 | Lactate threshold intervals | Speed endurance, tempo development |
| Phase 3 | 7–9 | VO2 max intervals | Maximal aerobic power |
| Phase 4 | 10–12 | Race-specific intervals | 5K pace specificity, competition preparation |

**Session frequency:** 3 running sessions per week. One interval session, one tempo or steady-state session, and one easy long run. The interval session is always the priority session of the week and should be placed when your client is freshest — typically mid-week after a rest day or easy day.

**Suggested weekly layout:**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Easy run or rest |
| Tuesday | Strength session A |
| Wednesday | **Interval session** |
| Thursday | Strength session B |
| Friday | Rest or easy walk |
| Saturday | Tempo or steady-state run |
| Sunday | Easy long run |

---

## Universal Session Protocols

These apply to every interval session in the programme without exception.

### Pre-Session Inhaler Protocol
Two puffs of SABA inhaler 15–20 minutes before the warm-up stride-outs begin. Not 15–20 minutes before the session starts — 15–20 minutes before the first hard effort. Time this carefully. The inhaler should be taken after the easy jogging portion of the warm-up and before the stride-outs, so that peak bronchodilation coincides with the beginning of the interval work.

### Extended Warm-Up for Interval Sessions (Minimum 15 Minutes)

*Minutes 1–4:* Easy walking transitioning to easy jogging. Nasal breathing throughout. Heart rate rising gently.

*Minutes 4–8:* Easy continuous jogging at RPE 10–11. Settle into a relaxed rhythm. Begin rhythmic breathing — 3 steps inhale, 2 steps exhale.

*Minutes 8–12:* Gradually increase pace to comfortable tempo (RPE 13) over 4 minutes. Not a sudden jump — a smooth, progressive increase.

*Minutes 12–15:* Six progressive stride-outs. Each stride-out is 20–25 seconds long. Stride-out 1 and 2: comfortable tempo pace. Stride-out 3 and 4: strong tempo pace. Stride-out 5 and 6: approaching interval pace. Full 60–90 second easy jog recovery between each stride-out. These final two stride-outs are the most important part of the warm-up for EIA management — they are the mechanism by which the refractory period is induced.

*After the final stride-out:* Rest 2–3 minutes of easy walking before beginning the first interval. This brief pause allows the heart rate to settle slightly and ensures the refractory period is fully established before the sustained hard efforts begin.

### Breathing Score Monitoring
Use the 1–5 breathing score throughout every interval session. After each interval, your client rates his breathing: 1 = completely normal, 2 = slightly aware of breathing but comfortable, 3 = noticeable tightness or wheeze, 4 = significant tightness affecting the effort, 5 = severe symptoms. Scores of 1–2 are normal and expected. A score of 3 means extend the recovery period before the next interval and monitor closely. A score of 4 means end the interval portion of the session, complete easy jogging only, and review before the next session. A score of 5 means stop immediately, administer the inhaler, and follow the emergency protocol.

### Recovery Intervals
The recovery periods between intervals are not passive rest — they are active easy jogging unless specified otherwise. Active recovery maintains blood flow, prevents the sharp drop in core temperature that can trigger bronchospasm, and keeps the airways warm. The one exception is in Phase 3 where some recoveries are walking — this is deliberate and explained in context.

### Cool-Down (Minimum 10 Minutes)
5 minutes of easy jogging transitioning to walking, followed by 5 minutes of static stretching. Finish with 2 minutes of diaphragmatic breathing. Monitor breathing for 15–20 minutes post-session. Late-phase EIA responses can occur up to 6–8 hours after exercise — advise your client to be aware of any chest tightness developing later in the day and to use his inhaler if needed.

### Session Log
Keep a written log of every interval session recording the following: weather conditions and temperature, pre-session inhaler timing, breathing scores after each interval, any modifications made, and how your client felt overall. This log is invaluable for identifying patterns — for example, whether symptoms are worse in cold weather, at certain times of day, or after certain foods — and for communicating with his GP if a medication review is needed.
